summary: Describes the VLS protocol from Cabletron, which supports equal-cost multipath routing and recalculates routes quickly when the topology changes. It is a vendor specification published as informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A map-sharing method for switches that splits traffic among equally good roads and quickly finds new roads when one closes.

questions: how do switches discover each other
subtitle: A protocol for switches to coordinate and find the best paths through a network fabric.

tldr.problem: Switches in a Cabletron fabric need to discover each other, maintain a consistent picture of the network topology, and calculate efficient paths for routing traffic between all switches with minimal protocol overhead.
tldr.mechanism: VLSP (Virtual LAN Link State Protocol) is a link-state routing protocol adapted from OSPF that runs at the MAC layer on switches. Each switch advertises its state, all switches maintain a database of the topology, and each switch calculates shortest paths to all others using Dijkstra's algorithm. VLSP supports equal-cost multipath routing for load balancing.
tldr.outcome: Switches can quickly adapt to topology changes (failed links or switches) and route traffic efficiently through the fabric. The protocol is optimized for switch operation by running at the physical layer and avoiding IP configuration requirements.

today: RFC 2642 is an Informational document describing Cabletron's proprietary VLS protocol. It is not an Internet standard and was specific to Cabletron's switch products. The protocol is now primarily of historical interest, though the concepts influenced later switch protocols.

sections.title: Introduction to VLSP
sections.content:
RFC 2642 specifies the Virtual LAN Link State Protocol (VLSP), part of Cabletron's InterSwitch Message Protocol (ISMP). VLSP is a dynamic routing protocol for determining and maintaining a fully connected mesh topology among switches in Cabletron's SecureFast VLAN (SFVLAN) product.

VLSP is derived from the OSPF routing protocol but adapted to work at the MAC layer (physical layer) rather than the IP layer. Each switch maintains an identical topological database and uses it to calculate loop-free paths to all other switches. The protocol supports equal-cost multipath routing (sending traffic along multiple paths of equal cost) and recalculates routes quickly when the topology changes.

Unlike OSPF, VLSP requires no IP configuration, runs entirely on MAC addresses, and assumes all switches exist in a single area with no interdomain routing.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a simplified version of a famous routing protocol called OSPF, but adapted to work on switches instead of routers and without needing IP addresses.

sections.title: Key Concepts and Data Structures
sections.content:
VLSP operates using three main data structures:

Interface Data Structure: Each switch port has an interface with a state (Down, Loopback, Point-to-Point, Waiting, DS Other, Backup, or DS). The interface tracks its type (point-to-point or broadcast), cost, neighboring switches, and timers. At startup, all links are assumed point-to-point; a link becomes multi-access (broadcast) if a second neighbor is discovered on it.

Neighbor Data Structure: Each switch maintains information about neighboring switches it communicates with, including their state and when they last sent messages. Neighbors transition through states: Down, Attempt, Init, Two-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading, and Full (adjacent).

Area Data Structure: VLSP does not support multiple areas like OSPF does. All switches exist in a single area. The database holds link state advertisements (LSAs) describing each switch's state and the links it is connected to.

A designated switch (DS) and backup designated switch (BDS) are elected on multi-access links to reduce the number of adjacencies and flooding overhead. Point-to-point links do not require a designated switch.
sections.plainLanguage: Each switch keeps track of its ports, its neighbors, and the network map. On shared connections (like a shared cable), one switch becomes the boss (designated switch) to reduce chatter.

sections.title: Protocol Operations
sections.content:
VLSP operates in four main stages:

Discovery Process: The VlanHello protocol notifies VLSP of neighboring switches. When a second neighbor is discovered on a link, the link type changes to multi-access and VLSP sends its own Hello packets to elect a designated switch and backup.

Database Synchronization: Once neighbors are discovered, adjacencies are formed and databases are synchronized. The two switches exchange Database Description packets to summarize their databases, followed by Link State Request packets to download missing advertisements. This reduces protocol traffic compared to flooding everything immediately.

Maintaining the Database: When a switch's state changes (an interface goes down or a neighbor fails), it originates a Link State Update packet containing new link state advertisements. These are flooded throughout the fabric using a reliable algorithm that tracks which switches have received each advertisement. Switches acknowledge receipt with Link State Acknowledgment packets.

Path Calculation: Each switch uses its link state database to run Dijkstra's algorithm, calculating shortest paths to all other switches. When equal-cost paths exist, VLSP can return up to three paths for multipath routing.
sections.plainLanguage: First, switches say hello to each other. Then they swap notes about the whole network. When something changes, they all hear about it quickly. Finally, each switch figures out the best routes to every other switch.

sections.title: Architecture and Design Differences from OSPF
sections.content:
VLSP differs from OSPF in several key ways:

MAC Layer Operation: VLSP runs at the physical MAC layer, not at the IP layer. This means it does not require IP address configuration on switch interfaces. Switches are identified by their 6-octet MAC address plus 4 octets of zeros. Interfaces are identified by a switch's MAC address plus a 4-octet port number.

No Multiple Areas: OSPF allows networks to be divided into areas to reduce routing overhead. VLSP assumes all switches exist in a single area with no level-2 routing or interdomain reachability, simplifying the protocol.

All Point-to-Point at Startup: VLSP assumes links are point-to-point initially and only treats a link as multi-access (broadcast) if multiple neighbors are detected on it. This avoids unnecessary Hello packet overhead on truly point-to-point links.

Path Information: Instead of just storing next-hop information like OSPF, VLSP calculates and returns complete end-to-end paths as lists of port identifiers, and can return up to three equal-cost paths.

No Configuration Required: VLSP requires no configuration parameters. Switches are automatically identified by their MAC addresses. OSPF requires IP address assignments. Path metrics are configurable but optional.

Features Not Supported: VLSP does not support periodic refresh of advertisements (optimizing traffic), routing based on type of service, external routing information, or authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: This protocol is simpler than OSPF in some ways: it does not need IP addresses, does not split networks into zones, and requires no setup. But it keeps all the key ideas: switches learn the topology and calculate paths.

sections.title: Protocol Parameters and Implementation
sections.content:
VLSP uses two types of timers: one-shot timers (expire once) and interval timers (expire at regular intervals). Timer granularity is one second. Interval timers should avoid drift (staying synchronized with each other) unless small random jitter is added.

Five packet types are defined: Hello packets (for discovering neighbors and electing designated switches), Database Description packets (summarizing database contents), Link State Request packets (requesting specific advertisements), Link State Update packets (delivering new advertisements), and Link State Acknowledgment packets (acknowledging receipt).

Two types of link state advertisements exist: Switch Link Advertisements (originated by every switch, describing its interface states) and Network Link Advertisements (originated by the designated switch on a multi-access link, listing all connected switches).

Implementation requires list manipulation primitives for managing link state advertisement lists, and tasking support to execute procedures immediately or schedule them for later execution.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol uses timers, five types of messages (hello, database summary, requests, updates, and acks), and two types of announcements (about individual switches and about shared cables).
